cards.title: Dequeue jQuery for logged-out front-end users
cards.claim: jQuery is necessary for logged-in users because the WordPress admin bar uses jQuery, but a logged-out user visiting the site has no reason to load jQuery; it can be removed with a code snippet that filters scripts and deregisters jQuery.
cards.action: Add a WPCodeBox snippet that filters WP and Q scripts and dequeues/deregisters jQuery, then use the condition builder so the snippet runs only on the front end and only when the user is not logged in.
applies_when: the site does not otherwise need jQuery for logged-out visitors
do_not_use_when: user is logged in, because the WordPress admin bar uses jQuery
front-end functionality depends on jQuery or jQuery migrate/dependencies
unknowns: whether the site's theme or plugins need jQuery for logged-out visitors
exact performance gain from removing jQuery
evidence_quotes: jQuery is actually loading for logged out users
It's necessary for loggedin users because the WordPress admin bar uses jQuery, but there's absolutely no reason that a logged out user should be loading jQuery when they visit our site
add a filter for WP and Q scripts. and we need to dq and dregister jQuery which will get rid of jQuery and jQuery migrate and all those dependencies
only to run if it's on the front end
it only runs if the user is not logged in

cards.title: Unload unneeded WooCommerce assets per page with Asset CleanUp
cards.claim: Asset CleanUp can unload specific WooCommerce files on a page where those features are not needed, while keeping WooCommerce assets active where they are needed; on the landing page in its current state, the WooCommerce category had 13 files and most were disabled.
cards.action: Activate Asset CleanUp, open the page, use its metabox to unload specific WooCommerce items such as brand styles, source buster, add to cart, block styles CSS, and jQuery block UI, optionally keep the WooCommerce coming soon CSS if not sure, then save.
applies_when: the page does not need the unloaded WooCommerce features in its current state
you want page-specific unloading rather than disabling WooCommerce globally
do_not_use_when: if you later add WooCommerce features to the page, such as a mini cart
if the page needs the unloaded WooCommerce assets
unknowns: whether the WooCommerce coming soon CSS file is actually needed
future page changes may require re-enabling unloaded assets
evidence_quotes: the easiest way to unload stuff like that on specific pages is a plugin called asset cleanup
you can see our Woo Commerce category here has 13 files
we don't need our brand styles. We don't need source buster. We don't need add to cart right now. We might in the future
We don't need the block styles CSS. We don't need the jQuery block UI
there is one thing here that I think I'm going to keep, and it's the WooCommerce coming soon CSS file. I'm not positive that we actually need it, but it's pretty small, so we'll keep it for now
Asset cleanup lets you kind of surgically remove things on specific pages while keeping stuff active where it needs to be

cards.title: Load Google Fonts locally instead of making external calls
cards.claim: Instead of embedding Google Fonts or making a call out to Google Fonts, download the font files, convert them to WAFT 2 files, upload them to WordPress, and switch font variables to the local versions.
cards.action: Download the desired Google Fonts, convert TTF files to WAFT 2 files using Font Squirrel web font generator or Google Web Fonts Helper, upload the WAFT 2 files through the theme/site builder's custom fonts option or a custom font plugin, specify weight and italic/normal, then change font variables to the local font names and save.
applies_when: the theme or site builder offers a custom fonts option, or a custom font plugin can be used
you want to avoid embedding or calls out to Google Fonts
do_not_use_when: if your builder or theme does not offer a way to upload custom fonts and no custom font plugin is used
if Font Squirrel does not successfully convert all desired fonts; the passage says it might be because one font is a variable font

exact performance benefit of local fonts
